source.title: Massive Stars: Some Open Questions and the role of Multi-Object Spectroscopy

accepted.question_text: What is the true upper stellar mass limit in nature for individual massive stars? Existing evidence from the Arches cluster suggests an upper limit of about 150 solar masses, but analyses of stars in the core of R136 in 30 Doradus infer initial masses between 160 and 320 solar masses, and the binary R144 may have had an initial system mass of about 400 solar masses, implying that at least one component could have reached about 200 solar masses at birth. The open problem is to determine whether the apparent masses above 150 solar masses are real and how much they are affected by model dependence, calibration uncertainties, and unresolved binarity.
accepted.context_brief: Upper mass limit of massive stars

evidence.quote: Figer (2005) determined in his study of the Arches cluster that the upper mass limit, the highest mass a star reaches in Nature, is about 150 M⊙.
More recently, however, Crowther et al. (2010) found initial masses between 160 and 320 M⊙ for stars a1, a2, a3 and c in the core of R136 in 30 Dor, with a1 being the record holder.

Very recently, Sana et al. (2013) have determined that the total present mass of the binary R144 in 30 Doradus is 200-300 M⊙, estimating that the initial mass of the system could be as high as 400 M⊙, which would mean that at least one of the components should have reached 200 M⊙ at birth.

accepted.question_text: Why do evolutionary masses and spectroscopic masses of massive stars still disagree, and what physical or modeling ingredients are needed to remove the remaining mass discrepancy? The unresolved issue is that masses inferred by placing stars in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and comparing with evolutionary tracks are still systematically inconsistent with masses inferred from stellar-atmosphere analyses of spectra, even after improvements such as line blanketing in atmosphere models and rotational mixing in evolutionary models. Current discrepancies are smaller than in the original reports, but they still persist at the level of about 20% to 50% across the Milky Way, the Large Magellanic Cloud, and the Small Magellanic Cloud.

evidence.quote: Although both techniques should give the comsistent masses, Herrero et al. (1992) showed that there is a systematic discrepancy between both (the mass discrepancy).

There have even been claims that the problem was solved thanks to these improvements (Weidner & Vink 2010), at least within errors. However, the literature is plaged with examples of the mass discrepancy.
Thus we may conclude that the mass discrepancy is still controversial and remains as a problem, but at a milder scale (20-50%) than when it was first detected.

accepted.question_text: What is the correct effective-temperature scale of O-type stars, especially in galaxies beyond the Magellanic Clouds, once the effects of small-number statistics, faint spectra, and model dependence are properly controlled? The paper argues that O-star temperature scales appear to become slightly hotter as metallicity decreases, but the comparison between galaxies can change depending on which stars are sampled, and for galaxies beyond the Magellanic Clouds the available data are very scarce. A further unresolved issue is that the commonly used scales rely on only two atmosphere codes, FASTWIND and CMFGEN, which use similar physical processes.

evidence.quote: Therefore we must realize that the comparison of results between different galaxies is subject to these effects of low number statistics. This is more certain for galaxies beyond the Magellanic Clouds, where the data are really scarce.

In the warning corner we shall include the fact that only two atmosphere codes have been used (FASTWIND and CMFGEN, see Santolaya-Rey et al. (1997); Puls et al. (2005); Hillier & Miller (1998)), with similar physical processes, and that the small number statistics may play a role for the limited samples available.

accepted.question_text: What is the correct effective-temperature scale of red supergiants, and how should stellar-atmosphere and evolutionary models be revised to reconcile the disagreement between temperatures inferred from TiO-band fitting and from spectral-energy-distribution and far-infrared methods? The paper identifies a persistent discrepancy between these two approaches and notes that it may arise because TiO bands form in upper atmospheric layers where opacity, structure, and three-dimensional effects are large. The related open issue is also whether the coolest effective temperatures reachable by red supergiants are strongly controlled by the adopted overshooting parameter in evolutionary models.

evidence.quote: However, Davies et al. (2013) fitting the Spectral Energy Distributions and using the Far Infrared Method obtain even higher temperatures than Massey et al. The discrepancy between both results can be attributed to the formation of TiO bands in upper layers, where opacity, structure and 3D effects are expected to be large.

Of course, this raises again a problem with the evolutionary models, although Davies et al. indicate that the position of the Teff limit in RSGs (i.e., the coolest Teff RSGs can reach) depends strongly on the adopted overshooting parameter and is thus very unceratin.

accepted.question_text: What physical effects are responsible for the mismatch between observed and theoretical mass-loss relations in massive stars, including the vertical offset in the wind momentum-luminosity relationship and the existence of weak winds below a limiting magnitude? The unresolved problem is to determine how much of this mismatch is caused by microclumping, macroclumping, porosity, and the inadequacy of traditional diagnostics such as Hα when mass loss is small, and how those effects should be incorporated into reliable mass-loss estimates.

evidence.quote: However, we identify two important problems in that figure: a vertical shift between the observed and theoretical relationships for all three galaxies and a limiting magnitude, below which the observed winds are weaker than theoretically expected.
Effects of wind clumping may be related to both points.
The classical diagnostic for mass-loss (the Hα line) is not only affected by clumping, but is also insufficient when trying to determine small mass-loss.

accepted.question_text: Does radiatively driven wind theory break down at very low metallicity, or can the apparently stronger-than-predicted winds reported in galaxies such as IC 1613, WLM, and NGC 3109 be explained by measurement systematics and abundance assumptions? The paper notes that some studies reported wind momenta stronger than expected at oxygen abundances around one-seventh to one-tenth solar, which would imply either a failure of the standard radiatively driven wind picture or the appearance of another wind-driving mechanism. At the same time, later work suggests that overestimated terminal velocities and assuming a solar alpha-to-iron ratio in galaxies with subsolar alpha-to-iron ratios may remove the conflict, but the sample sizes remain too small for a firm conclusion.

evidence.quote: This would indicate a breakdown of the RDW theory when the metallicity is very low (or alternatively, the emergence of another mechanism driving more efficiently the wind at very low metallicities, see Lucy (2012)).

Thus, Tramper et al. results may be explained by a combination of overestimated terminal velocities and an assumed metallicty derived from oxygen together with the assumption of a solar α/Fe ratio (whereas the analyzed galaxies seem to have a subsolar α/Fe ratio).
Nevertheless, we must remember that we are in the realm of low number statistics: the number of analyzed objects is still worringly small.
More analyses of objects in low metallicity galaxies are needed, particularly in galaxies with independent evidence of a solar α/Fe ratio.

accepted.question_text: Why are high-mass red-supergiant progenitors of core-collapse supernovae apparently missing, and is the correct explanation enhanced red-supergiant mass loss, direct dark core collapse to a black hole, or some other evolutionary channel? The unresolved problem arises because observations matched to standard evolutionary calculations place the initial masses of post-red-supergiant core-collapse supernova progenitors well below the roughly 25-solar-mass value expected for more massive progenitors. The paper suggests that stronger red-supergiant mass loss could reconcile models with observations, but it also raises the alternative possibility that stars above about 20 solar masses may collapse directly into black holes with no supernova or only a very faint event.

evidence.quote: Mass-loss rates are poorly known for RSGs and usually empirical, highly uncertain formulae are used (see Smith 2014).

Smartt et al. (2009), comparing observations to standard evolutionary calculations, conclude that the initial masses of post-RSG core collapse SNe progenitors range between 8±1.0 and 16.5±1.5 M⊙, clearly below the expected value of 25 M⊙.
With enhanced mass-loss rates, the initial masses obtained for RSGs exploding as SNe would be higher, thus reconciling observations and models

Alternatively, may be that stars more massive than about 20 M⊙ suffer a dark core collapse, i.e., form directly a black hole without SN explosion (or with a very faint event, see Smartt et al. (2009)).

accepted.question_text: What process is primarily responsible for bringing nuclear-processed material from the interior of early massive stars to their surfaces? The paper shows that surface helium and CNO abundance patterns are real, but the exact mechanism remains unclear because rotational mixing, binary interaction, magnetic braking or magnetic-field effects, and inner instabilities can all produce similar observational signatures. The open problem is to identify second-order diagnostics, such as parameter correlations or time scales, that can separate these scenarios in a consistent way.

evidence.quote: Thus we conclude that nuclear processed material is brought to the surface of early massive stars, but the exact process responsible for it is not clearly identified (as all of them will produce a similar pattern) and we have to look for second order differences (like correlations between parameters or time scales).
While rotational mixing and binary interaction can probably account qualititively for all cases, other processes like magnetism and inner instabilities have still to be addressed in a consistent way.

accepted.question_text: Do the fastest-rotating massive stars actually undergo homogeneous evolution, and if so, what unambiguous observational evidence would demonstrate it? The paper notes that the highest observed projected rotational velocities in Galactic and 30 Doradus O stars are high enough that homogeneous evolution should be expected, but it also states that there is still no firm observational evidence supporting that evolutionary channel.

evidence.quote: if it is high enough, evolution proceeds homogeneously: the star has a constant abundance profile and it evolves towards the left from the Zero Age Main Sequence.
We note that although the highest velocities found in the MW and specially in the the LMC are sufficient to expect homogeneous evolution, there are still no firm evidences supporting it.

accepted.question_text: What is the physical origin of macroturbulent line broadening in massive O and B stars? The paper states that this broadening mechanism is real but of unknown origin, that the commonly suggested explanation in terms of kappa-driven gravity-mode pulsations does not explain many high-mass stars, and that alternative ideas involving turbulent pressure from subsurface convection or convection-driven internal gravity waves remain under investigation. The unresolved issue is whether one of these mechanisms dominates or whether several processes contribute in different parts of parameter space.

evidence.quote: Besides the well known mechanisms that we find in textbooks (like the natural, Doppler or the different collisional broadening mechanisms) spectral lines in massive O and B stars are affected by a brodening mechanism of still unknown origin. It is usually called macroturbulence
Thus this kind of pulsations do not seem to explain the presence of macroturbulent broadening in high-mass stars

Recently, Grassitelli et al. (2015) propose that turbulent pressure, originated by sub-surface convective layers, may be at the root of this extra broadening and Aerts & Rogers (2015) conclude that it may be explained by convection-driven internal gravity waves (IGW)

accepted.question_text: Do post-red-supergiant blue loops actually produce a distinct population of B supergiants, and can that scenario explain the mismatch between observed and predicted surface abundances in candidate post-red-supergiant objects? The paper notes that some blue supergiants have pulsational properties consistent with post-red-supergiant structures, but their abundance enhancements are much smaller than predicted by non-standard evolutionary models, and there is still no observational evidence for two separate B-supergiant populations. A related observational challenge is that post-red-supergiant B supergiants should rotate much more slowly than pre-red-supergiant ones, so testing the idea requires accurate rotational velocities at or below about 5 km s−1.

evidence.quote: The observed abundances of post-RSG candidates (i.e., B-supergiants having pulsational properties expected for post-RSG stellar structures) are still clearly smaller than those predicted by the non-standard evolutionary calculations.
And there are still no observational evidences supporting the presence of two different populations among B-supergiants (as it would be the case if post-RSG blue loops do exist).

Post-RSG B-supergiants should have much lower rotational velocities than their pre-RSG counterparts. However, this would imply to be able to determine accurate rotational velocities at very low levels, at or below 5 km s−1.
